questions.question: What is the primary role of conditional statements in computer programming?
options: To declare new variable names in memory
To allow a program to make decisions and execute specific code paths based on conditions
To repeatedly run a block of code an infinite number of times
To convert numeric data types into string characters
questions.hint: Conditions allow code to choose between different actions depending on whether a statement is TRUE or FALSE.
questions.explanation: Conditional statements allow a program to evaluate logical tests (which return TRUE or FALSE) and make decisions, selecting which instructions to execute accordingly.

questions.question: Under what condition will the body code inside a basic 'if (condition) { ... }' block execute in R?
options: Only when the condition evaluates to TRUE
Only when the condition evaluates to FALSE
Every time the script runs regardless of the condition
Only when the condition evaluates to NA or NULL
questions.hint: The word 'if' checks for truth before running its enclosed instructions.
questions.explanation: In R, an 'if' block executes its body code if and only if the enclosed test condition evaluates to a single logical TRUE.

questions.question: What happens when the condition in an 'if' statement evaluates to FALSE and there is no 'else' block provided?
options: R throws a fatal runtime syntax error and halts
R automatically restarts the computer session
R simply skips the block and continues running the next instruction after the closing brace
R prints a default warning message to the console
questions.hint: Without an alternative fallback branch, R simply bypasses the unfulfilled condition.
questions.explanation: When an 'if' test evaluates to FALSE and no 'else' block is attached, R simply skips the code inside the curly braces and continues with subsequent lines of code.

questions.question: Why is an 'else' block attached to an 'if' statement in R?
options: To define optional function arguments
To execute an alternative fallback block of code when the 'if' condition evaluates to FALSE
To force the 'if' condition to repeat until it becomes TRUE
To import external statistical packages into R
questions.hint: It provides a two-way decision: one path for TRUE and an alternate path for FALSE.
questions.explanation: An 'if...else' construct provides a two-way branch: the 'if' block executes when the condition is TRUE, and the 'else' block executes when the condition is FALSE.

questions.question: In an 'if ... else if ... else' ladder, how does R evaluate multiple conditions?
options: It evaluates all conditions simultaneously and executes all matching branches
It evaluates conditions randomly until one succeeds
It evaluates conditions sequentially from top to bottom, executes the first TRUE branch, and skips all remaining branches
It only evaluates the final 'else' branch
questions.hint: Think of a waterfall: the first gate that opens takes the flow, and lower gates are bypassed.
questions.explanation: R checks conditions in order from top to bottom. As soon as one condition evaluates to TRUE, its corresponding code executes and the entire remaining chain is skipped.

questions.question: Why is the order of conditions critical when grading student marks with 'else if'?
options: Because R reads code from bottom to top
Because if an overly broad condition like 'marks >= 40' is placed before 'marks >= 90', top scores will enter the lower grade branch first
Because 'else if' requires conditions to be alphabetically sorted
Because R cannot compare numbers greater than 50
questions.hint: Since R stops at the first TRUE condition, broader or lower thresholds must not precede higher, specific thresholds.
questions.explanation: Because R executes the first TRUE condition it encounters, placing 'marks >= 40' first would cause a mark of 95 to immediately match 'Pass' or 'Grade C', never reaching the 'Grade A+' branch.

questions.question: What is a 'nested if' statement in R programming?
options: An 'if' statement that has been deprecated in modern R versions
An 'if' statement placed inside the code block of another 'if' or 'else' block
An 'if' statement that only accepts complex numbers as inputs
A vector of conditions defined inside a list
questions.hint: Nesting means placing one container or control block inside another.
questions.explanation: A nested 'if' statement is an 'if' (or 'if...else') construct placed inside the body of an outer 'if' or 'else' block, enabling multi-stage hierarchical decisions.

questions.question: What will the following code return: switch('coffee', tea = 'Selected Tea', coffee = 'Selected Coffee', juice = 'Selected Juice', 'Invalid')?
options: 'Selected Tea'
'Selected Coffee'
'Selected Juice'
'Invalid'
questions.hint: The switch() function compares the first argument against the named option keys.
questions.explanation: The switch() function matches the input string 'coffee' with the named parameter 'coffee' and returns its corresponding value: 'Selected Coffee'.

questions.question: When switch() is passed an integer index such as switch(2, 'Apple', 'Banana', 'Cherry'), which option is returned?
options: 'Apple'
'Banana'
'Cherry'
NULL
questions.hint: R uses 1-based indexing for positional matching.
questions.explanation: When the first argument to switch() evaluates to an integer, it uses 1-based positional selection: 1 returns 'Apple', 2 returns 'Banana', and 3 returns 'Cherry'.

questions.question: How does the vectorized 'ifelse()' function differ fundamentally from a standard 'if...else' statement in R?
options: 'ifelse()' can only process string text, while 'if' only processes numbers
'if...else' is used for single scalar control-flow decisions, whereas 'ifelse()' evaluates conditions element-by-element across vectors
'ifelse()' is slower and cannot be used in data analysis pipelines
There is no difference; 'ifelse()' is simply a shorter alias for 'if...else'
questions.hint: Consider what happens when you test an entire vector of 1,000 numbers at once.
questions.explanation: Standard 'if...else' controls single-path program execution for a scalar logical value, while 'ifelse(test, yes, no)' is vectorized and returns a vector with elements selected based on each individual test element.

questions.question: What are the three required arguments in the syntax of 'ifelse(test, yes, no)'?
options: variable, operator, value
logical condition vector, value returned if TRUE, value returned if FALSE
minimum limit, maximum limit, step size
input file, output file, log path
questions.hint: The first is the test condition, followed by results for truth and falsehood.
questions.explanation: The syntax is ifelse(test, yes, no), where 'test' is the logical condition vector, 'yes' is the return value for elements where test is TRUE, and 'no' is the return value for FALSE elements.

questions.question: Which logical operator should be used in an 'if' control-flow condition to perform scalar short-circuit AND evaluation in R?
options: %and%
and
questions.hint: Double ampersand performs scalar short-circuit evaluation ideal for single-test control statements.
questions.explanation: The '&&' operator evaluates from left to right examining only the first element, short-circuiting if the first condition is FALSE. It is designed for scalar control-flow statements like 'if'.

questions.question: What common beginner mistake occurs in the code: if (temperature = 30) { print('Hot') }?
options: Using single '=' (assignment) instead of '==' (equality comparison) inside the condition
Forgetting to import the temperature library
Using double quotes instead of single quotes
Printing text without a cat() function
questions.hint: A single '=' attempts to store a value into a variable rather than checking if two values are equal.
questions.explanation: In R, '=' is an assignment operator. Testing equality requires the comparison operator '=='. Using '=' in an 'if' condition produces a syntax error.

questions.question: In Machine Learning workflows, why are conditional statements applied to model prediction probabilities (e.g. if (prob >= 0.80))?
options: To retrain the neural network automatically
To translate raw floating-point prediction probabilities into concrete actionable decisions or class labels
To clean missing values from the training dataset
To speed up GPU matrix multiplication
questions.hint: Models predict probabilities like 0.87, but an app needs to decide: 'Approve Loan' or 'Flag as Spam'.
questions.explanation: Machine learning classifiers output continuous probability scores between 0 and 1. Decision logic (like thresholding at 0.80) maps these probabilities into discrete business actions or classifications.

questions.question: In standard R scripts, where must the 'else' keyword be placed relative to the closing curly brace '}' of the preceding 'if' block?
options: On the same line as the closing brace: '} else {'
At the very beginning of the next script file
Anywhere in the script; whitespace and newlines are always ignored in interactive parsing
Inside the parentheses of the condition
questions.hint: In interactive R console parsing, placing 'else' on a new line causes R to consider the 'if' block complete before seeing 'else'.
questions.explanation: In R interactive sessions, placing 'else' on a new line after '}' causes R to execute the complete 'if' statement and subsequently fail with 'unexpected else'. Always write '} else {' on the same line.
